description_long: On March 15, 2025, simultaneous with the VOA shutdown, the Trump administration terminated federal grants to Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty (RFE/RL), Radio Free Asia (RFA), and the Middle East Broadcasting Networks. RFE/RL had been founded in 1950 to counter Soviet propaganda and broadcasts to countries including Russia, Ukraine, Belarus, and Central Asia. RFA broadcasts to China, North Korea, and Southeast Asia. RFE/RL president Steve Capus said the termination would be a massive gift to America's enemies, many of whom are already celebrating. RFA president Bay Fang called it a reward to dictators and despots, including the Chinese Communist Party. Czech Republic Foreign Minister Jan Lipavský immediately sought EU backing to maintain RFE/RL operations from its Prague headquarters. USAGM's funding terminations had Kari Lake's signature. A senior official at one of the networks told NPR: We would bleed out. Prior funding freeze attempts during Trump's first term had been halted by courts. Russian and Chinese state propaganda celebrated the grant terminations. The combined networks had reached over 420 million people weekly across more than 100 countries in 63 languages.

title: FCC Forces ABC to Suspend Jimmy Kimmel Over Charlie Kirk Monologue
description_short: FCC Forces ABC to Suspend Jimmy Kimmel Over Charlie Kirk Monologue
description_medium: FCC chair Brendan Carr pressured broadcasters after Jimmy Kimmel's remarks about Charlie Kirk's death, and affiliates moved to preempt the show before ABC suspended it. Carr's public statements, affiliate decisions, and ABC's action should be distinguished, while the sequence raised concerns about government pressure on editorial expression.
description_long: On September 17-18, 2025, FCC Chairman Brendan Carr appeared on a conservative podcast and threatened to revoke ABC affiliate broadcast licenses if they continued airing Jimmy Kimmel Live! — citing Kimmel's Monday monologue suggesting Trump supporters were exploiting the death of Charlie Kirk. Within hours of Carr's threats, Nexstar Media Group (operator of 28 ABC affiliates, with its $6.2 billion Tegna merger requiring FCC approval) announced it would preempt the show indefinitely. Sinclair Broadcast Group (38 ABC stations, also with pending FCC regulatory matters) followed. ABC parent Disney, which was seeking FCC approval for ESPN's NFL Network acquisition, then suspended Kimmel indefinitely. Trump called it Great News for America. FCC Democrat Anna Gomez said Disney had faced clear government intimidation. The ACLU, Writers Guild, SAG-AFTRA, and dozens of lawmakers condemned the suspension as government-compelled censorship. After protests in California and national outcry, Disney reinstated Kimmel on September 22. CBS had canceled The Late Show with Stephen Colbert under comparable circumstances months earlier, also coinciding with its $16 million Trump settlement and FCC merger approval. Both Colbert and Kimmel were TV's two most vocally anti-Trump late-night hosts.

description_long: In late February 2026, FBI Director Kash Patel fired a dozen agents and staff from CI-12, the bureau's Washington-based counterintelligence unit, after discovering that his own phone records and those of White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles had been subpoenaed by FBI investigators as part of Special Counsel Jack Smith's probe into Trump's classified documents. The timing was catastrophic: the firings occurred just days before the United States launched major military operations against Iran on February 28, 2026. Among those fired was a section chief who handled espionage threats from the Iranian government and its proxies; most of the purged agents worked on foreign counterintelligence cases including active Iran-related operations. One source told CBS News the firings were devastating to the FBI's Iran program, noting the terminated agents maintained confidential human informants in Iranian communities that you can't replicate with new agents — these sources will go away. Patel had already relocated up to 1,500 FBI employees out of Washington, fragmented the bureau's counterterrorism and cyber divisions, and overseen the firing of senior officials on political grounds, systematically dismantling the institutional infrastructure the FBI had spent a generation rebuilding after its post-9/11 failures.

title: Trump Proposes Ending Birthright Citizenship — Blocked by Courts
description_short: Trump Proposes Ending Birthright Citizenship — Blocked by Courts
description_medium: Trump's January 20, 2025 executive order sought to deny recognition of birthright citizenship to specified children born in the United States whose parents lacked permanent immigration status. Several federal judges blocked enforcement while constitutional challenges proceeded. The immediate dispute concerned the Fourteenth Amendment and the president's power to change longstanding citizenship rules through executive action rather than legislation or constitutional amendment.
description_long: On January 20, 2025, Donald Trump signed an executive order purporting to end birthright citizenship for children born in the United States to parents without legal immigration status or who are in the country on temporary visas — a direct challenge to the 14th Amendment to the Constitution, which grants citizenship to all persons born on U.S. soil. Multiple federal courts immediately blocked the order, with one judge calling it 'blatantly unconstitutional.' The administration appealed to the Supreme Court, which refused to fully stay the lower court injunctions while the litigation proceeded. Constitutional scholars from across the political spectrum — including prominent conservatives — agreed the order directly contradicted the plain text of the 14th Amendment as consistently interpreted for 150 years. The order was widely viewed as a deliberate provocation designed to force a Supreme Court reconsideration of birthright citizenship.

Even as Trump's conservative Supreme Court majority granted him broad immunity and limited courts' ability to block his policies nationwide, he continued attacking federal judges who ruled against him as biased and illegitimate. The Supreme Court's actions in Trump's favor included rejecting efforts to remove him from ballots, limiting obstruction charges against January 6th defendants, granting presidential immunity from criminal prosecution, and restricting courts' power to issue nationwide injunctions against his policies. Despite benefiting from these rulings by his own appointees, Trump maintained his attacks on the judiciary as a 'deep state' institution, creating a two-tiered system where courts that helped him were legitimate while those that constrained him were corrupt. title: Three US Citizen Children Deported to Honduras With Their Mothers
description_short: Three US Citizen Children Deported to Honduras With Their Mothers
description_medium: In late April 2025, the Trump administration deported three young children who were US citizens to Honduras, alongside their undocumented Honduran mothers. Both mothers had been summoned to routine meetings with officials in Louisiana as part of the Intensive Supervision Appearance Program — an ICE check-in system — and were detained and deported within hours or days.
description_long: In late April 2025, the Trump administration deported three young children who were US citizens to Honduras, alongside their undocumented Honduran mothers. Both mothers had been summoned to routine meetings with officials in Louisiana as part of the Intensive Supervision Appearance Program — an ICE check-in system — and were detained and deported within hours or days. Their US citizen children were removed with them. Legal experts told CNN the deportations underscored the slapdash approach of the administration's deportation campaign, which ran up against the constitutionally protected parental rights of some undocumented adults and the full legal rights of their US citizen children. The administration's stated position was that removing children with their deported mothers was the humane option — that separating children from deported parents would be worse — while simultaneously pursuing policies that led to family separation in other contexts. Critics noted that the government did not provide adequate time, process, or legal counsel for the families to make meaningful decisions about their US citizen children's futures before deportation. Immigration law scholars noted this created a scenario where the United States was effectively forcing its own citizens into exile in a foreign country. The cases contributed to growing legal battles and congressional demands for accountability over the treatment of US citizen children caught in the administration's mass deportation machinery.

title: Trump Posts Buy Signal Before Tariff Pause: Potential Insider Trading
description_short: Trump Posts Buy Signal Before Tariff Pause: Potential Insider Trading

description_long: On April 9, 2025, at 9:37 a.m., President Trump posted on Truth Social: THIS IS A GREAT TIME TO BUY!!! DJT — using the ticker symbol for Trump Media & Technology Group, his majority-owned company. Less than four hours later, Trump announced a 90-day pause on nearly all global tariffs. The S&P 500 gained 9.5% by day's end, recovering approximately $4 trillion in market value — about 70% of the value destroyed over the previous four trading days. Trump Media (DJT) surged 22.67%, far outpacing the broader market, despite being a company that lost $400 million the prior year with no relation to tariff policy. Legal experts noted that Trump's post, if made while he already planned the tariff pause, would constitute trading on insider information — a federal securities violation. Government ethics law professor Kathleen Clark at Washington University said: He's sending the message that he can effectively and with impunity manipulate the market. Securities law expert Richard Painter, a former White House ethics lawyer, said people who bought when they saw the post made a lot of money and questioned whether Trump was already planning the announcement. Trump retained approximately 53% ownership of Trump Media, meaning any stock price surge directly enriched him personally.

title: Insurrection Act Threat - Military Deployment Against Americans
description_short: Insurrection Act Threat - Military Deployment Against Americans
description_medium: Trump's border-emergency directive required the defense and homeland security secretaries to assess whether use of the Insurrection Act was warranted. The request raised concerns about expanding military involvement in domestic enforcement. A required assessment is distinct from actual invocation of the law, deployment under it, or a declaration of martial law.
description_long: Donald Trump included a provision in his January 20th border emergency executive order requiring the Secretaries of Defense and Homeland Security to report within 90 days on whether to invoke the Insurrection Act of 1807, creating the framework for using military forces against American civilians despite his advisors' resistance. The 217-year-old law would give Trump 'broad and vague authority to deploy troops - either with or without the request of a state - to suppress any insurrection, domestic violence, unlawful combination, or conspiracy,' effectively allowing him to impose martial law for mass deportations and protest suppression. Despite Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem reportedly recommending against invocation due to low border crossings, Trump's inclusion of the Insurrection Act review kept the threat alive for future use. Twenty-two Senate Democrats introduced emergency legislation to restrict Trump's authority under the act, with Senator Mark Warner stating that 'Though he has not yet invoked the Insurrection Act, his threats to do so indicate a pressing need for congressional reform.' The proposed reforms would require congressional approval for use longer than seven days and provide judicial review to prevent abuse, while clarifying that the law 'cannot be used to suspend habeas corpus, impose martial law, or deputize private militias.' Friends Committee on National Legislation warned that invocation would enable 'mass disappearances and suppress protest in a huge abuse of presidential power.'

title: Rally Superspreader Events - 700+ COVID Deaths Linked
description_short: Rally Superspreader Events - 700+ COVID Deaths Linked
description_medium: A Stanford study estimated that 18 Trump campaign rallies between June and September 2020 were associated with more than 30,000 additional coronavirus infections and over 700 deaths. The figures were modeled estimates comparing affected communities, rather than a direct count of attendees who died. The findings highlighted potential public-health costs of campaign gatherings.
description_long: A Stanford University study found that Donald Trump's campaign rallies during the COVID-19 pandemic led to over 30,000 coronavirus infections and more than 700 deaths, making them superspreader events that prioritized political theater over public health. The study analyzed 18 Trump rallies held between June 20 and September 22, 2020, finding that communities hosting rallies experienced significant increases in COVID cases and deaths compared to similar communities that didn't host events. Despite warnings from health experts that large gatherings without masks or social distancing would spread the virus, Trump continued holding rallies with thousands of packed, unmasked supporters throughout the pandemic. The campaign required attendees to undergo temperature checks and provided masks and hand sanitizer, but Trump rarely wore masks himself and crowds largely ignored safety protocols. Three of the studied rallies were held indoors, further increasing transmission risk, while Trump mocked mask-wearing and social distancing as weakness or political theater. The superspreader rallies demonstrated Trump's willingness to sacrifice American lives for campaign events, treating public health measures as obstacles to his political ambitions rather than life-saving precautions. Communities that hosted Trump rallies paid a deadly price, with the Stanford researchers concluding that 'the communities in which Trump rallies took place paid a high price in terms of disease and death.' The rallies became symbols of Trump's reckless disregard for public health during a global pandemic that killed over 400,000 Americans on his watch.

title: Birthright Citizenship Executive Order - Constitutional Amendment by Decree
description_short: Birthright Citizenship Executive Order - Constitutional Amendment by Decree
description_medium: Trump's January 2025 executive order sought to restrict recognition of birthright citizenship for certain U.S.-born children based on their parents' immigration status. Legal challengers argued that it conflicted with the Fourteenth Amendment, and judges blocked implementation. The dispute concerned the order's legality, rather than an executive amendment changing the Constitution.
description_long: Donald Trump signed an executive order attempting to end birthright citizenship through presidential decree, targeting U.S.-born children whose parents lack citizenship or permanent immigration status in direct violation of the Fourteenth Amendment's constitutional guarantee that 'all persons born or naturalized in the United States...are citizens of the United States.' The January 20th order declared that after February 19, 2025, citizenship would only be granted to babies if at least one parent is a U.S. citizen or lawful permanent resident, representing an unprecedented attempt to rewrite the Constitution through executive action. Multiple federal judges issued preliminary injunctions blocking the order from taking effect, with the Legal Defense Fund and ACLU successfully arguing that the president cannot unilaterally overturn constitutional amendments ratified in 1868 to repudiate the Dred Scott decision. The order targeted children born to parents with temporary visas, asylum seekers, undocumented immigrants, and other legal statuses, potentially creating a class of stateless children born on American soil but denied citizenship rights. The NAACP Legal Defense Fund warned that if implemented, the order 'could deny citizenship to U.S.-born children if neither of their parents has citizenship or permanent immigration status,' violating the core principle of jus soli that has governed American citizenship since the Civil War era. The Supreme Court confirmed birthright citizenship in United States v. Wong Kim Ark (1898), establishing that children born in the U.S. to immigrant parents were entitled to citizenship regardless of their parents' status.
